target.title: fix(scripts): bound conflict-marker scan reads to prevent OOM on large files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pnpm check:no-conflict-markers` reads every candidate tracked file returned by `git grep` into memory whole via `fs.readFileSync`. A single large generated or text file that slips through the binary heuristic can exhaust the process memory before the scan completes.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Cap each scanned file at `MAX_CONFLICT_MARKER_SCAN_BYTES` (50 MiB).
- Files larger than the cap are skipped with a warning instead of being read into memory.
- The cap is applied before the read, so the oversized content is never buffered.
- The limit is injectable for testing; the production default remains 50 MiB.

## User Impact

- Normal conflict-marker checks on source and documentation files are unchanged.
- Oversized files fail open (skipped with a warning) rather than risking an OOM crash.
- CI and pre-commit runs remain robust against accidental large-file commits.

## Evidence

Local focused test passes:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts --run
```

Result:

```
✓ |tooling| test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts (5 tests) 98ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Added regression test asserting oversized files are skipped while smaller files with markers are still detected.

Real behavior proof:

```bash

console.log('readCount:', readCount);
console.log('warnings:', warnings);
fs.unlinkSync(tmpFile);
"
```

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown; 1 MiB is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: IDENTITY_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts`.
- Added regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` covering normal load and an oversized file that exceeds the cap.
- Local test run:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
  # 9 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof

I created a workspace with an oversized `IDENTITY.md` (2 MiB) and ran `loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`. The loader returns `null` instead of buffering the oversized file:

- Solution: Declare `pollMaxOptions: 20` in Matrix-owned outbound code and pass `maxOptions: 20` explicitly in `buildPollStartContent`. The shared `normalizePollInput` helper's public contract is unchanged: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit, preserving caller-controlled behavior.
- What changed:

  - `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.ts` — `buildPollStartContent` passes `maxOptions: 20` explicitly
  - `src/polls.ts` — restored public helper contract (no global default)
- What did NOT change: `normalizePollInput` omitted-limit semantics; other channel implementations.

## ClawSweeper review fixes

**P1: Keep the generic poll limit caller-configured** — Restored `normalizePollInput` public contract: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit (preserving existing behavior for all callers). The 20-option Matrix protocol limit now lives in Matrix-owned code: `matrixOutbound.pollMaxOptions = 20` and `buildPollStartContent(..., { maxOptions: 20 })`. Channels that already declare their limits (Discord=10, WhatsApp=12, etc.) are unaffected. Third-party and generic gateway callers that omit `maxOptions` retain their existing behavior.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Matrix polls were missing the 20-option protocol limit. Now enforced at the Matrix boundary.

Both `listRunsForRequesterFromRuns` and `listRunsForControllerFromRuns` spread the full `Map.values()` into an intermediate array before filtering. For registries with thousands of records, this allocates a full-size intermediate array that is immediately discarded.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `[...runs.values()].filter(...)` pattern creates two allocations: the spread array holding all records, then the filtered result. Replacing with a direct `for...of` loop + conditional `push()` eliminates the intermediate array entirely.

target.body:
Fixes #6615. Supersedes #92456 (author inactive since 2026-06-12, no response to review, conflicts with main — full credit to @Hidetsugu55 for the STOP-list concept and dual-host enforcement approach, both kept here).

## Update — re-review 2 (clawsweeper P1 blockers resolved)

The previous review's three P1 blockers were "contract declared but not wired." All three are now wired end-to-end, with focused tests on each exact path plus refreshed real-behavior proof. Also merged latest `origin/main` (resolves the CONFLICTING/behind-main note).

- **[P1] Wire `tools.exec.denylist` into config schema + gateway caller** — `denylist` added to the strict zod `ToolExecBaseShape` (`src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts`, non-empty-pattern refinement) so `openclaw config validate` accepts it and rejects malformed entries; threaded as `execConfigDenylist` through `agent-tools.ts` → `bash-tools.exec.ts` → `processGatewayAllowlist`, unioned across global + per-agent layers (`resolveEffectiveExecDenylist`). Tests: `config.schema-regressions.test.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts`.
- **[P1] Pass denylist hits into node-host `system.run`** — `invoke-system-run.ts` now evaluates the effective denylist (openclaw.json global + per-agent + `exec-approvals.json` file layer) and passes `denylisted`/`denylistReason` into `evaluateSystemRunPolicy`; the model auto-reviewer is hard-blocked on a hit (human-only), and unanalyzable commands fail closed. Tests: `invoke-system-run.test.ts` (+ node denial reason `denylist-hit`).
- **[P1] Add denylist to exec-approval protocol writes** — `ExecApprovalsDenylistEntrySchema` + `denylist` added to `ExecApprovalsPolicyFields` in `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/exec-approvals.ts` so `exec.approvals.set` / `exec.approvals.node.set` round-trip the field. Tests: `exec-approvals-validators.test.ts`.

Two extra hardening changes made while wiring the above:

- **Real defect fix:** `sanitizeExecApprovalPolicy` (`src/infra/exec-approvals.ts`) was silently dropping the defaults-layer `denylist` on every `saveExecApprovals` write — a routine policy write would disarm an operator's STOP list. Now normalized and preserved.
- **Standalone gate:** the gateway host now has an independent `requiresDenylistApproval || …` short-circuit in `processGatewayAllowlist`, so the deny-over-allow guarantee cannot regress even if `requiresExecApproval`'s denylist handling ever changes.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's exec approvals support allowlists but no denylist: there is no way to force human approval (or denial) for specific dangerous commands when an agent runs at `security=full` / `ask=off`, or when a broad allowlist/durable trust would otherwise auto-approve them. #6615 asks for a deny-over-allow screening layer so commands like `git push --force` or `rm -rf` patterns always require an explicit human decision, regardless of permissive settings.

## Fix

- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.ts`: entry normalization, strict validation (`collectExecDenylistErrors`), and `resolveEffectiveExecDenylist` (de-duplicated union across layers — deny anywhere = deny).
- **Both config layers**: `openclaw.json` `tools.exec.denylist` (global + per-agent) **and** `~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json` (defaults + `*` + agent), wired through both exec hosts (see Update above).
- **Shared pattern language**: denylist patterns reuse the existing allowlist glob compiler via a new `matchesExecGlob` export — no second matcher to keep in sync (`*` → `[^/]*`, `**` → `.*`, `?` → `[^/]`).
- **Deny wins first**: a hit forces approval ahead of `ask=off`, `security=full`, allowlist hits, and durable allow-always trust, on both the gateway exec host and node-host `system.run` (node denial reason `denylist-hit`). Explicit allow-once approval still clears a hit; `security=deny` still wins overall.
- Conservative fallback: unanalyzable command + configured denylist ⇒ approval required, not fail-open. Basename variants and `bash -c "..."` inner payloads are screened.

## Evidence

**Typecheck (repo's real TS-Go checker):** `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` both clean on this branch. (Stock `tsc` throws a bogus TS4058 in `src/secrets/config-io.ts` that tsgo does not — pre-existing on `main`.)

**Focused tests — all green on the exact paths flagged:**
- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts` — 19 (normalize/dedupe, both-layer union, exact/glob/basename/wrapper matches, conservative fallback, precedence).
- `src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts` — 19 and `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.test.ts` — 36 (node-host `system.run` enforcement, config-layer union, human-only, `denylist-hit`).
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts` — 54 (gateway standalone denylist gate at `security=full`/`ask=off`).
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/exec-approvals-validators.test.ts` — 8 (protocol/file denylist round-trip).
- `src/config/config.schema-regressions.test.ts` — 39 and `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` — 23 (config schema accept/validate + label/help coverage).

> Note: on a host that symlinks `head` to cargo-coreutils, one unrelated pre-existing test (`processGatewayAllowlist > uses a plan-backed enforced command…`) fails on a `/usr/bin/head` vs `/usr/lib/cargo/bin/coreutils/head` path assertion. It is environmental and independent of this PR (our diff to that test file is additive only).

**Real behavior proof** (real decision code path via `node --import tsx`, no test doubles — `git push --force origin main` allowlisted + durable-trusted at `security=full`/`ask=off`, denylist supplied through the openclaw.json config layer exactly as the wired callers do):

```
## BEFORE (control: no denylist configured)
[gateway-host] command="git push --force origin main" security=full ask=off allowlisted=true durable=true -> AUTO-RUN
[node-host]    command="git push --force origin main" -> ALLOWED

## AFTER (denylist configured via openclaw.json tools.exec.denylist)
denylist = [{"pattern":"git push*--force*","reason":"history rewrite"}]
[gateway-host] -> APPROVAL REQUIRED
[node-host]    -> DENIED (denylist-hit)

## AFTER + explicit allow-once approval
[node-host]    -> ALLOWED (approval cleared the hit)
```

## Scope notes

- Contract is now complete across config schema, gateway protocol write schema, gateway host caller, node-host `system.run`, docs/help (`schema.help.ts` + `schema.labels.ts`), tests, and real proof.
- No drive-by refactors.


## Node-host prompt parity (b0164f0fe8a, 2026-07-09)

Review found that the `host=node` `security=full`/`ask=off` fast path invoked `system.run` directly before prepare/approval registration, so a denylist STOP rule hard-denied server-side (`denylist-hit`) instead of raising the documented human allow-once prompt.

Fixed for prompt parity (recommended option):

- The direct fast path is taken only when the caller-visible effective denylist is **known empty**: the `openclaw.json` config layer is empty AND the node approvals-file denylist (fetched via `exec.approvals.node.get`) is known and empty. Fetch failures fail **closed** into the prepare path.
- On the prepare path, the effective denylist (config layer + node approvals-file layer) is evaluated caller-side; a hit forces a registered human approval request even at full/off, mirroring the gateway host: auto-review is excluded (human-only), and `allow-always` is downgraded to one-shot so no durable trust can be minted from a denylist hit.
- Non-matching commands with a configured denylist still auto-run (via the prepare path); setups with no denylist keep the direct fast path.

Focused tests added in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts`: config-layer hit registers an approval request (no direct denial), approvals-file hit registers an approval request, non-matching denylist auto-runs, known-empty denylist keeps the fast path, approvals fetch failure fails closed to prepare. `vitest run src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts --pool=forks` => 4 files, 146 tests passed; tsgo typecheck clean.

Honest proof status: production decision-function proof and the focused node-host approval-registration tests are in; a live gateway+node prompt -> allow-once -> runs-exactly-once capture is being prepared on a dedicated QA host and will be appended when complete.

Known residual (intentional, documented here): a denylist configured ONLY in the node machine's own local `openclaw.json` remains invisible to the gateway-side caller and still hard-denies server-side (fail-closed). The two operator surfaces this PR documents (`tools.exec.denylist` config layer and the exec-approvals file) now both get prompt parity on host=node.

target.title: fix(commitments): avoid quadratic heartbeat session discovery
target.body:
Related: #105787

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where heartbeat commitment fan-out loads and expires the commitments store under the queue/file lock, then scans the returned records once for every qualifying due record. When many due records belong to one session, that post-lock quadratic work increases heartbeat latency. Reported isolated medians were approximately 191 ms at 1,000 records, 847 ms at 2,000, and 2.28 s at 4,000.

## Why This Change Was Made

The commitments store now builds the rolling 24-hour sent-count map once per agent and reuses it for due-session discovery and single-session due selection. The due-window, snooze, expiry, daily-cap, ordering, limit, agent-scope, queue, and cross-process file-lock behavior remain on the existing path.

This is intentionally an interim JSON-store fix. OpenClaw's shared SQLite state schema already contains a commitments table and indexes, but making it canonical requires a separate JSON-to-SQLite migration/doctor contract and broader persistence coverage. That migration remains a follow-up rather than expanding this focused latency fix.

## User Impact

Heartbeat commitment discovery changes from repeated full-store counting to one aggregation pass plus the existing due-record scan. Large concentrated sessions therefore scale linearly with store size instead of quadratically, without changing which sessions are eligible for delivery.

## Evidence

- Added a correctness test covering due-window filtering, snoozes, rolling daily caps, agent scope, and sorted session keys.
- Added a concentrated-session scaling test with 8,000 due records in one session and one recent sent record. It uses the production-like `limit: 10`, so the base implementation scans all qualifying records and repeatedly rescans the store; the fixed implementation reuses one count map.
- Added a runner-level proof using the production `startHeartbeatRunner` and `runHeartbeatOnce` path, a real temporary JSON state directory, 16,000 concentrated due records, and one recent sent record. target.title: fix(ui): unblock stale-chunk recovery when the document probe hangs
target.body:
Related: #104304

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Control UI users can remain on a stale hashed-chunk error after a gateway update when the document `HEAD` probe never settles. Automatic recovery and the Retry action both wait on that probe, so the fallback route revalidation cannot run.

On current `main`, the probe had no deadline or abort signal, and automatic/manual callers started independent probes. A temporary deterministic regression check on that behavior failed in three ways: no abort signal was passed, concurrent callers made two requests, and the router Retry path made a second probe instead of reaching fallback revalidation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stale-chunk recovery owner now uses one bounded document probe with an explicit `AbortController`, a 3-second timer, and `finally` cleanup. Concurrent automatic and manual callers share the same in-flight promise; identity-checked cleanup releases the busy state after settlement so later retries can probe again. The deadline is below the existing 5-second attempt cooldown, preventing a timeout-driven re-render from immediately starting another probe.

This PR was AI-assisted. The implementation, callers, tests, dependency contract, and final branch diff were inspected against the repository guidance; fresh autoreview reported no accepted or actionable findings.

The abort behavior follows the platform contract documented by [MDN for `AbortController.abort()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController/abort) and the [Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-method), where aborting the controller rejects the fetch. An explicit owned timer is used instead of `AbortSignal.timeout()` because native timeout scheduling was not controlled by this repository's Vitest/jsdom fake timers; the explicit timer makes the deadline and cleanup deterministic.

## User Impact

The stale-chunk panel now settles a hung document probe within 3 seconds. Automatic and manual recovery do not duplicate the request, and Retry can reach route revalidation after the probe aborts. Existing build guards, cooldown behavior, successful reloads, and offline no-reload behavior remain unchanged. There is no config, protocol, or rendered-layout change.

target.title: fix: keep yielded parent runs deferred until subagents settle
target.body:
## Summary

This change promotes yielded-parent semantics into a shared parent lifecycle classifier and routes the affected cron, subagent-registry, and Discord/source-message paths through that state instead of letting each consumer infer completion from terminal-shaped model-attempt events, missing final text, or abort-shaped control flow.

The shipped behavior is:

- yielded parent + active descendants is treated as waiting/deferred, not ordinary completion;
- yielded parent + no descendant is treated as diagnostic error;
- cron delivery waits for a real final outcome instead of counting the yielded attempt as `ok / not-delivered`;
- Discord/source-message progress remains parent-owned while the yielded parent is waiting;
- descendant settlement wakes/reconciles yielded parents through the existing continuation paths.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where parent-agent runs that spawned child sessions/subagents and then called `sessions_yield` could look finished before the parent task actually completed.

The most visible failures were:

- isolated cron `agentTurn` jobs with valid delivery targets could finish as `ok / not-delivered` because the yielded parent had no final payload yet;
- Discord source-message lifecycle could clear parent progress/done indicators while child work was still active or while the parent was waiting to reconcile final output;
- run history/status surfaces made yielded parent work look like delivery failure, ordinary success with no output, or completed source-message work instead of a paused/resumable parent lifecycle.

`session_yield` is supposed to end the current model turn, not the parent task. This PR makes that distinction explicit for the affected runtime consumers.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

Operators and developers can now rely on `sessions_yield` after spawning child/subagent work without the parent run being misrepresented as complete at the cron or Discord lifecycle boundary.

Practically:

- autonomous development crons stop inflating misleading `ok / not-delivered` results for intentionally yielded runs;
- cron history exposes a distinct `deferred` state for yielded parent handoff;
- Discord progress no longer marks the parent source message done just because the parent yielded while children continue;
- yielded parent runs are resumed/reconciled when descendant work settles;
- debugging points to the parent/child lifecycle state instead of falsely implying delivery target resolution failed.

## Linked Context

- #95535 — `sessions_yield` isolated cron resumption/delivery gap.
- #92369 — subagent orchestration in isolated cron sessions needs reliable spawn/wait/aggregate semantics.
- #92116 — `sessions_yield` completion delivered as passive context can break orchestration loops.
- #86537 — subagent terminal reconciliation can expire suspended final delivery.
- #86538 — session write-lock timeouts can block subagent delivery lanes.
- #95833 — subagent abort-settle/session-lock failure can break session continuation.
- #92460 — isolated cron completion delivery gap around final controller return.
- #95604 — Discord subagent progress visibility.
- #94153 — durable queued subagent completion announcements.
- #95847 — requester-consumed descendant completion accounting.

## What Changes

### Shared parent lifecycle state

- Adds `src/agents/agent-lifecycle-parent-state.ts`.
- Classifies lifecycle events with explicit yielded/waiting vs terminal semantics.
- Exports the classifier through `openclaw/plugin-sdk/reply-runtime`.
- Routes subagent registry and Discord source-message handling through the classifier instead of local `yielded && paused` inference.

### Cron lifecycle and delivery

- Adds first-class cron run status `deferred`.
- Classifies yielded descendant handoff before delivery-mode branching, so text, structured payloads, `delivery.mode: none`, source-satisfied delivery, and normal direct delivery all share the same semantics.
- Prevents duplicate/interim parent announcements while descendants are active.
- Records yielded-without-descendant as explicit error diagnostic.
- Keeps deferred manual task runs active rather than failing them.
- Disables one-shot deferred cron jobs after handoff to avoid retry loops.

### Persistence, protocol, CLI, and UI

- Extends run-log JSON/SQLite encoding and status filtering for `deferred`.
- Extends Gateway protocol schemas and cron server filters.
- Extends CLI status/wait typing and docs.
- Extends hook-visible status typing.
- Adds Control UI status/filter labels and generated locale fallbacks.

### Parent/subagent reconciliation

- Tracks yielded/paused parents that still have pending descendants.
- Marks yielded parents with `wakeOnDescendantSettle` so they are resumed/reconciled when descendant work settles.
- Handles child success/failure settlement through existing subagent lifecycle recovery paths.
- Adds regression coverage for yielded parents being reconciled after child failure so diagnostics can wake the parent.

### Discord/source-message lifecycle

- Projects lifecycle events from agent execution into reply/channel handling.
- Uses the shared classifier to identify yielded/waiting parent state.
- Preserves in-progress/progress representation for yielded parents with active children.
- Avoids prematurely marking Discord status reactions done or clearing draft/progress state when the parent yielded and remains waiting.

### Concurrent user-message semantics

`docs/tools/subagents.md` documents the selected policy: if a human sends another message while a requester is yielded, the new message starts a normal turn for the same requester session. OpenClaw keeps the yielded run visible as waiting on descendant completion rather than converting it into a stale final reply; when descendant completion arrives, the completion event is handed back to the requester for synthesis.

target.title: fix(agents): prevent subagent registry resurrection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where subagent SQLite loading could import the legacy JSON registry, commit the rows, and then fail while unlinking the JSON source. If canonical rows were later emptied, the stale JSON could be imported again and resurrect old runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Legacy import now runs only from automatic doctor/state migration. The runtime loader reads SQLite only. Imported rows and a durable `migration_sources`/`migration_runs` receipt commit in one synchronous SQLite transaction; source cleanup runs afterward and remains retryable on `EPERM` or process interruption. Stable source identity, content guards, and a durable skipped receipt prevent changed or ambiguous legacy files from being reinterpreted as new canonical state.

## User Impact

After migration, runtime reads cannot fall back to `runs.json`. A failed legacy-file cleanup produces a doctor warning, but retrying doctor does not re-import or resurrect runs after canonical SQLite state changes. Legacy files that cannot be verified or are ambiguous remain in place for operator recovery.

## Evidence

- Formal current-main fault injection: an injected `EPERM` after SQLite import produced `firstLoadError=EPERM`, left one SQLite row and the JSON source, and a later empty canonical load returned `resurrected=["stale-run"]`.
- Added deterministic coverage in `src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts` for v1 import, canonical-state skip, `EPERM` cleanup retry, changed/unreadable source handling, and post-commit crash recovery.
- Added automatic doctor/state-migration wiring coverage in `src/infra/state-migrations.test.ts`.
- Static validation passed: `oxfmt --check`, focused Oxlint, and `git diff --check`; fresh repository autoreview completed with no accepted/actionable findings.
- Focused Vitest execution was attempted with `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts src/agents/subagent-registry.persistence.test.ts src/agents/subagent-registry-state.test.ts`, but this isolated worktree has no `node_modules` and the wrapper exited with `OPENCLAW_MISSING_VITEST`.
- Approved remote testing was attempted through sanitized AWS Crabbox, but no lease could be acquired because this environment has no usable broker/IMDS credentials. PR CI is the remaining remote execution path.

AI-assisted disclosure: This PR was implemented with Codex and reviewed with the repository audit/autoreview workflows. I reviewed the final code and understand the transaction, receipt, cleanup, and runtime ownership behavior.

Limitations: a pre-receipt release could have imported JSON and lost its rows before this receipt existed; SQLite cannot reconstruct that historical provenance after both the rows and receipt are gone. This change fails closed for an unreceipted source when canonical rows already exist by recording a skipped receipt and preserving the JSON; an already-empty database from that historical state remains a manual-recovery case.

target.title: fix(deepgram): validate realtime base URL overrides, preserving ws(s):// endpoints
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a malformed Deepgram `baseUrl` in provider config crashes realtime
transcription session setup with an uncaught `TypeError: Invalid URL`, while an unrelated scheme
(e.g. `ftp:`) is silently accepted and rewritten into an unusable endpoint.

`normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` in `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts`
only trimmed the value — it never confirmed the result was a usable URL. Its consumer
`toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` does `new URL(normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl(config.baseUrl))` and then
rewrites the protocol for the WebSocket connection.

**Concrete example:** with `baseUrl: "not a url"`, `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` on current
`main` returns `"not a url"` and the downstream `new URL("not a url")` throws an opaque
`TypeError: Invalid URL` at session setup. A value like `ftp://host` parses but is not a usable
Deepgram endpoint, yet is accepted and rewritten.

## Why This Change Was Made

Validate the base URL at the normalizer boundary and **fail actionably**: only an absent/blank value
(or unset `DEEPGRAM_BASE_URL`) falls back to the default endpoint; an explicit value that is
unparseable, or whose scheme is none of `http:`/`https:`/`ws:`/`wss:`, throws a clear
`Invalid Deepgram baseUrl` error. This mirrors the sibling ElevenLabs fix (#105163).

The allowlist intentionally includes the WebSocket schemes: the released provider (`v2026.6.11`)
passes a direct `ws://`/`wss://` override straight through to `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl`, and Deepgram
realtime streaming itself is WSS — so custom proxies legitimately configure a `wss://` endpoint.
`toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` now preserves an explicit `ws:`/`wss:` scheme (only `http:`/`https:` are
mapped to their WebSocket equivalents), keeping that released behavior intact. Validation errors are
redacted — they never echo the raw configured URL, so embedded userinfo or credential-bearing query
params are not disclosed to logs/diagnostics.

## User Impact

**Before:** a mistyped Deepgram `baseUrl` surfaces an opaque `TypeError: Invalid URL` at session
setup; an unrelated scheme is accepted and produces an unusable endpoint.

**After:** an explicit malformed or unrelated-scheme `baseUrl` fails fast with an actionable,
secret-safe error; absent/blank config still defaults; valid `http(s)://` and direct `ws(s)://`
endpoints (including custom path/port) are unchanged.

## Evidence

- `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts` — `normalizeDeepgramRealtimeBaseUrl` accepts `http/https/ws/wss`, rejects unparseable and unrelated-scheme values (throws), and only defaults absent/blank input; error messages surface only "value is not a valid URL" or the offending `protocol`, never the raw URL. `toDeepgramRealtimeWsUrl` preserves a direct `ws:`/`wss:` scheme. Exposed via the existing `testing` object for coverage.
- Regression test: `extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.test.ts` — asserts absent/blank → default, valid `http(s)` → normalized, direct `wss://` and `ws://` → preserved, custom path + port on a `wss://` override → preserved through the URL builder, explicit malformed → throws, `ftp:` → throws `unsupported scheme`, and a `baseUrl` with userinfo + `api_key` query is rejected without its secret appearing in the error. These fail on the pre-fix trim-only version.
- Function probe against the real production helpers (via `testing`):

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import('./extensions/deepgram/realtime-transcription-provider.ts').then(m => …)"
--- direct wss:// override (released behavior) ---
normalize: wss://api.deepgram.com/v1
wsUrl    : wss://api.deepgram.com/v1/listen
--- wss:// custom proxy w/ path + port ---
wsUrl    : wss://proxy.example.com:9090/dg/v1/listen
--- http(s):// still mapped ---
https -> wss://custom.example.com/listen
http  -> ws://localhost:8080/listen
--- malformed + unrelated scheme still rejected (redacted) ---
"not a url"               -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: value is not a valid URL
"ftp://files.example.com" -> THROWS: Invalid Deepgram baseUrl: unsupported scheme "ftp:" (expected http, https, ws, or wss)
```

(The credential-bearing `ftp://user:sup3r-secret@…?api_key=leak-me` input is rejected with no `sup3r-secret` / `leak-me` / `api_key` in the message.)

target.body:
Closes #105440

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where MIME detection treated generic ZIP/octet-stream bytes inconsistently across media families: image extensions and headers were correctly overridden by the sniffed generic container, but audio and video extensions/headers could still win and mislabel ZIP-like bytes as `audio/*` or `video/*`.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a sniff returns a generic container (`application/zip` or `application/octet-stream`), extension and header MIME claims for image, audio, and video are now untrusted together. Document refinements that intentionally map ZIP containers (for example XLSX) remain trusted. Focused regression coverage was added for audio/video path and header cases.

## User Impact

Attachments and local media that are generic containers with misleading audio/video filenames or content-types are classified as the sniffed container type, matching the existing image policy. Legitimate Office Open XML documents that are ZIP-based still resolve via extension refinement.

## Evidence

**Verification host:** local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

Closeout:
- `git diff --check` — pass
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check packages/media-core/src/mime.ts packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts` — pass
- `pnpm exec oxlint packages/media-core/src/mime.ts packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts` — pass (0 warnings/errors)
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts` — **123 passed**
- `pnpm check:changed` started but expanded into long `tsgo:core:test`; stopped and replaced with path-scoped static checks above (`closeout_fast_adjust` / heavy_expand)

Pre-fix main contrast (same ZIP buffer, different paths via `detectMime`):

```text
image  => application/zip
audio  => audio/mpeg          # bug
video  => video/mp4           # bug
xlsx   => application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet
```

Post-fix:

```text
image  => application/zip
audio  => application/zip
video  => application/zip
xlsx   => application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Generic ZIP sniff no longer lets audio/video extension or header MIME override the container; image and XLSX behavior stay correct.
- Environment: local macOS, openclaw checkout at branch tip, Node via `pnpm exec tsx` and `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Current-main contrast: On main, generic ZIP + `.mp3` / `.mp4` returned `audio/mpeg` / `video/mp4` while `.png` correctly returned `application/zip`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. Build a plain ZIP buffer with JSZip (`hello.txt` only).
  2. Call `detectMime({ buffer, filePath })` for `/tmp/fake.png`, `/tmp/fake.mp3`, `/tmp/fake.mp4`, `/tmp/file.xlsx`.
  3. Run `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts`.
- Evidence after fix: audio and video paths return `application/zip`; xlsx still returns the spreadsheet MIME; all 123 mime unit tests pass including new audio/video regression cases.

## What Problem This Solves

When a skill is installed globally via ClawHub (`~/.openclaw/skills/<slug>`), its lockfile entry lives at `~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`, not in the workspace's `.clawhub/lock.json`. `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` was passing only the workspace lockfile to `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` for every skill, including global ones. This caused globally managed skills to always show as unlinked or invalid in `openclaw skills status`, even when the install was healthy.

Fixes #105530

## Why This Change Was Made

`readClawHubSkillsLockfileStatusSync` reads `<dir>/.clawhub/lock.json` for a given directory. Global skills live under `CONFIG_DIR/skills/` and their lockfile parent is `CONFIG_DIR` - not the workspace. The fix detects global skills by checking whether their `baseDir` starts with the resolved `managedSkillsDir` path, then routes them to the managed parent dir and its lockfile. The managed parent dir also satisfies `resolveWorkspaceSkillInstallDir` correctly so the install path check inside `resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync` passes too.

## User Impact

Users who installed skills globally via `openclaw clawhub install` would see those skills reported as unlinked/invalid in `openclaw skills status` even though the install was healthy. After this fix the status correctly shows `linked`.

## Evidence

New test in `src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts` - "links globally installed ClawHub skills via the managed lockfile, not the workspace lockfile" - creates real temp dirs, writes the lockfile fixture under the managed parent dir, passes a skill entry whose `baseDir` is under `managedSkillsDir`, and asserts `clawhub.status === "linked"`.

target.title: fix(abort): cancel active ACP detached tasks on requester stop
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stopping an agent session would leave ACP detached tasks (spawned via `sessions_spawn` with the ACP runtime) running as orphans. Users stopping an active session could have background ACP child processes continue consuming CPU or memory indefinitely.

Fixes #105228

## Why This Change Was Made

`stopSubagentsForRequester` only traversed the subagent run registry (`listSubagentRunsForController`) to find children to cancel. ACP spawns create task records in the task registry under `ownerKey: requesterInternalKey` instead, making them invisible to the subagent run path. The fix enumerates active ACP tasks via `listTasksForOwnerKey` after the existing subagent run loop and fires a best-effort `cancelSession` for each non-terminal task not already handled. `AcpSessionManager.cancelSession` handles session/run mode semantics internally so persistent-session runtimes are not indiscriminately killed. `seenChildKeys` deduplicates across both paths.

## User Impact

Stopping an agent session now also cancels active ACP background tasks it owns. Previously those tasks could remain running after the parent session was stopped.

## Evidence

Two new tests in `src/auto-reply/reply/abort.test.ts`:

- `stopSubagentsForRequester cancels active ACP detached tasks not in the subagent registry` — verifies `cancelSession` is called for an active ACP task when no subagent runs exist
- `stopSubagentsForRequester skips terminal ACP tasks and tasks already covered by the subagent registry` — verifies terminal tasks and tasks whose child key was already handled by the subagent run loop are not double-cancelled

Releasing a reused ChatGPT Responses WebSocket deleted `websocketSessionCache` by session id without checking whether a newer same-session connection already owned that slot. A stale release could close/evict a valid replacement connection.
